A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same VideoHallu study. Methods, result tables, figures, equations, and appendix showcases can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original VideoHallu evaluations, GRPO fine-tuning and curriculum experiments in Tables 1–2, and qualitative hallucination cases.

after.justification: v3 retains the original benchmark and fine-tuning results in Tables 2–3 and adds quantitative analysis by question type in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Both versions use Qwen2.5-VL-7B, GRPO, the Answer-Equivalence BERT embedding-similarity reward, individual dataset training, and GRW/PRW-to-SR curricula. v3's formal benchmark description does not establish a changed algorithm or training procedure.

E1.justification: The seven video-generation sources, four benchmark categories with 13 subcategories, and general-real-world, PhysBench, and VideoHallu training coverage are retained. Appendix C presents a question-type breakdown of VideoHallu rather than establishing added datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Table 1 and v3 Table 2 contain the same 20 model rows; v3 corrects the prose's earlier count of 16. The fine-tuning comparisons also retain the same baselines and variants. Appendix C uses six models already compared in v1.

E3.justification: The reported split changes from 800 training/1,525 test QA pairs to 800/2,433, reconciling the stated total of 3,233. v3 also resolves v1's conflicting 4,500/3,000 GRW descriptions to 3,000 and drops the stated greater-than-five-word restriction on judge-validation samples. These reported protocol revisions do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a focused diagnostic comparison of commonsense-only, counterintuitive, and unaided critical-thinking questions, extending v1's illustrative commonsense-versus-video case. Figure 1 revises the introductory case to watermelon videos. The training ablations and all 13 appendix hallucination showcases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained human–GPT agreement check and new question-type scores do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the two main result tables are retained, including Qwen2.5-VL-32B's 51.4% and PRW+SR-R1-7B's 54.2%. New Table 6 reports 100.0% commonsense-only, 46.8–53.1% counterintuitive, and 10.0–23.3% critical-thinking accuracy across six models. Figure 1 also supplies revised VideoScore results and model responses for different example videos.

T1.justification: v3 Section 2 introduces contextual-distance and text-mapping definitions and a constrained objective maximizing model–human answer disagreement while requiring text-only agreement and human-detectable video inconsistencies. This is a limited new formalization; the reward equation is retained, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion refocus the work on counterintuitive QA and critical-thinking-based abnormality detection, including claims that targeted training improves these abilities. v1's explicit greater-than-20-percentage-point perception/reasoning gap claim disappears. The benchmark contribution, roughly 50% baseline accuracy, and approximately 3% training gain remain.

C2.justification: v3 removes v1's substantial explanations based on visual-encoder bottlenecks, architectural differences, a scaling plateau beyond 7B, and nonsemantic ROUGE rewards. Interpretation centers instead on language-prior-biased critical thinking. Appendix C adds an explanation based on contextual hints versus unaided anomaly detection and a tentative CoT-benefit interpretation; the conclusion additionally identifies fine-tuning and compute costs as limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix B replaces v1's illustrative multiple-choice prompt with explicit CoT and direct-answer templates, including output tags and reflection instructions. v3 explicitly reports 987 generated videos, describes the repository as providing code rather than data, and removes Figure 4's separate video-example link. These are documentation and access-information changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds Prometheus-Vision, EVQAScore, and CG-Bench, while removing citations including FactScore, HallusionBench, HAL-Eval, and ROUGE. The motivation shifts toward QA-based evaluation and abnormality detection, but the central positioning against predominantly real-world video hallucination research remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten and condensed. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 4, detailed category descriptions move into Appendix A, and the appendices are reorganized around categorization, prompts, question-type analysis, and retained showcases. This exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned, Figure 4 is redrawn, and the radar charts receive revised sizing and legend layouts. v3 adds a taxonomy table and question-type results table and replaces the single prompt example with two template tables. Main displays and appendix showcases are extensively repositioned, although the showcase content is retained.

improvement.justification: v3 provides clearer organization, more usable prompting documentation, and a diagnostic breakdown that better distinguishes commonsense knowledge from video-grounding failures. These yield a modest improvement over v1. The gains remain limited: unchanged main scores are not reconciled with the revised test count, Appendix C lacks subgroup counts and a controlled CoT comparison, and the separate video-example link is removed.
